attribution.note: Marcus's own words describing Musk's FII remarks. The Musk quotes are context, not the claim.

semantics.note: A faithful past-tense observation that Musk's 10,000x extrapolation ignored data and compute bottlenecks and LLM limits.

contract.note: The plain reading (Musk did not raise these limits in that session) is ordinary and fair. Scope of 'never considering' is flagged as an ambiguity.

evidence.note: Fortune confirms Musk made the 10x claim at FII on that date. It says nothing about whether he mentioned bottlenecks.

reviews.rationale: Settling this needs a full transcript or recording of Musk's FII8 session, and the packet has none. The only item confirms the setting but not whether he raised data, compute or LLM limits. The evidence does not settle it either way.

attribution.note: Marcus quotes his own comment to Decrypt and endorses it in his post. The 2040 robot prediction is Musk's, used only as the target.

semantics.note: Compound claim: a track record of overoptimistic predictions (observation) plus a judgment that the 2040 humanoid prediction is another. Calling it overoptimistic implies it will not come true by 2040.

contract.note: Reading 'no different' as rejecting the 2040 crossover is ordinary, given 'Fat chance'. Measuring 'overoptimistic' by missed deadlines is the evaluator's choice, which is reasonable.

evidence.note: Reuters documents repeated missed FSD autonomy deadlines. This backs the track-record part but not the 2040 forecast that governs the outcome.
Tesla's own filing shows full self-driving was still a future goal in early 2021. This corroborates the missed timelines.

reviews.rationale: The track-record part has some support from the documented FSD deadline misses. Under the contract, though, the 2040 humanoid forecast governs the outcome, and that deadline has not passed. No conclusive event exists: no verified crossover. So the combined claim cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Marcus's own parenthetical remark in his post.

semantics.note: A causal chain: GenAI power use sustains fossil fuels, which benefits oil-rich countries. 'Even if never reliable' is kept as a qualifier.

contract.note: Splitting it into two parts and treating 'oil-rich' as fossil exporters is an ordinary reading. The period up to the post date is the evaluator's choice and is reasonable.

evidence.note: Dominion's 2023 reversal on retiring a coal plant, citing data-centre demand, partly supports part 1. The demand cited is for data centres generally, not GenAI specifically.
A 2025 IEA projection that gas will help meet data-centre demand. It is later and forward-looking, so context only.

reviews.rationale: Part 1 has partial support: one pre-post coal reversal tied to data-centre growth. Part 2, the benefit to oil- or gas-exporting countries, has no evidence at all. The IEA primary pages were unreadable. The packet does not establish the full causal claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own rhetorical question, answered firmly with 'Certainly not'.

semantics.note: A firm observation that OpenAI's own data does not show o1 as 100x better than GPT-4. The 'by their own data' qualifier is kept.

contract.note: Using OpenAI's launch-post ratios against GPT-4o is a fair, ordinary reading of 'their own data'.

evidence.note: OpenAI's AIME figures (74% vs 12%) give about a 6x gain, far below 100x. Company data is the very measure the claim names.
The Appendix A gains run from about 1.03x to 8x (e.g. GPQA 1.4x, CodeForces percentile 8x). None comes near 100x.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI's own o1 launch benchmarks show gains over GPT-4o of at most about 8x on any reported metric, nowhere near 100x. This holds as of the post date, so the claim is supported.
